quiz: A customer’s dog has no vest. Can you ask them to leave for that reason?
Yes, service dogs must be marked
No, a vest isn’t required
Only if the dog is large
Federal law doesn’t require a vest, tag, or harness.
Which question are you allowed to ask?
What’s your disability?
Can I see its certification?
What task is the dog trained to perform?
You may ask only if it’s a service animal required because of a disability, and what task it’s trained to do.
A customer says the dog is an emotional support animal. What applies?
Your normal pet policy
You must let it in
Ask for a doctor’s note
Emotional support animals aren’t service animals under the ADA.
Another customer is allergic. What should you do?
Ask the handler to leave
Offer the allergic customer a different table
Make the dog wait outside
Allergies aren’t a reason to deny access. Try to give both people space.
The dog keeps barking and the handler doesn’t stop it. You can:
Ask that the dog leave, and offer to serve the person without it
Call the police right away
Charge a cleaning fee
A dog that’s out of control can be removed, but you must offer service without the dog.
Can you charge a pet fee for a service dog?
Yes, the same as pets
Only in hotels
No, but you can charge for real damage
Surcharges aren’t allowed. Actual damage can be billed like any customer.
The dog is a pit bull, and your city bans the breed. You can:
Refuse because of the breed
Judge the dog by its behavior, not its breed
Require a muzzle
Breed bans can’t be used to keep out a service dog.
A guide dog is leading a blind customer. Should you ask the two questions?
Yes, always
No, its job is obvious
Only if it has no vest
Don’t ask when the dog’s role is obvious.
Can a service dog go into your kitchen?
Yes, anywhere
No, only areas open to customers
Only if it’s small
Service dogs go where customers can go. Food prep areas stay off limits.
A manager wants the handler gone and suggests saying “we’re closing early.” Is that OK?
Yes, it avoids a fight
No, a made-up excuse is still discrimination
Only after 8 p.m.
Using a false reason to remove someone because of their service dog is still discrimination.

start.q: Is it obvious what the dog does for the person? For example, a guide dog leading someone who is blind, or a dog pulling a wheelchair.

ask.q: Ask the two questions: “Is the dog a service animal required because of a disability?” and “What work or task has it been trained to perform?” Did they say yes and name a task?
ask.note: Accept their answers. If they describe something the dog does, such as alerting or interrupting, that counts. They don’t need exact words. Don’t ask for papers, a vest, a demonstration, or details about the disability.

control.q: Is the dog under control and housebroken? Look for lunging, repeated barking, jumping on people, or going to the bathroom inside.

correct.q: Ask the handler to get the dog under control. Did that fix it?

welcome.text: **Welcome them in.** Serve them like any other customer. Don’t charge a fee, seat them apart, or ask more questions. If another customer complains or is allergic, offer that customer a different spot.

notsd.text: **It isn’t a service dog under the ADA.** If they said it’s an emotional support or comfort animal, or said no to the first question, your normal pet policy applies. Some states also protect dogs in training, so check your state card. Say it kindly: “Thanks for telling me. Only service dogs can come inside, but I’m happy to help you another way.” Offer curbside, a patio if pets are allowed there, or to hold their order.

remove.text: **You may ask that the dog leave.** Say: “I’m sorry, the dog needs to step outside. We’re still happy to help you.” You must offer to serve the person without the dog, such as finishing the order or holding it while someone else watches the dog. Write down what the dog did.

scripts: “Welcome in! Quick question, is that a service dog required because of a disability? … And what task is it trained to do? Great, thanks. Enjoy your visit.”
They say it’s an emotional support animal
“Thanks for letting me know. Our policy only allows trained service dogs inside, but I’d be glad to help you with curbside pickup or hold your order.”
“Excuse me, I need to ask you to get your dog under control, please.” If it continues: “I’m sorry, the dog needs to step outside. We’re still happy to help you.”
“That’s a service animal, and the law allows it here. I’d be happy to move you to another table.”
An employee is allergic or afraid
Have a different employee serve that customer. Don’t ask the handler to leave or wait outside.
You’re not sure what to do
“Give me just a moment, I’m going to check with my manager.” Then use the decision guide in this app. Don’t guess, and don’t make up a reason like “we’re closing.”
